title: Dimensional Modeling I — Facts & Dimensions (kick off the Project Charter; design the pricing star schema)
gaps: G2 — Cannot translate a business question into a dimensional model: the learner defaults to one flat table and cannot separate measurable events (facts) from descriptive context (dimensions), so downstream marts become un-joinable and un-auditable. This week SEEDS-and-CLOSES the core fact-vs-dimension distinction.

G1 — Weak carry-over from relational theory (W13): the learner knows normalization rules but cannot decide WHEN to denormalize for analytics. Closed here by contrasting the 3NF source shape vs. the star-schema serving shape on the same CMS/NPPES data.

G9 — Cannot frame technical work as a business data product (no problem statement, no named persona, no KPIs). This week SEEDS the living Project Charter (Maria + 4 KPIs) so every later week has a money/risk/compliance anchor.
objectives: Given raw CMS Hospital Price Transparency and NPPES fields, classify each column as a FACT MEASURE, a DIMENSION ATTRIBUTE, or a DEGENERATE attribute and defend each call in one sentence (target: correctly classify at least 90% of a 25-column sample).

Design a star schema for the pricing domain: one price/charge FACT plus PROVIDER, PROCEDURE, FACILITY, and PAYER dimensions, each with a named surrogate key and at least one candidate business (natural) key.
Author Project Charter v0.1 stating Maria's problem in five sentences or fewer, naming the persona, and defining 4+ measurable KPIs, each with a formula and a grain-of-measurement note.
Explain, with a concrete CMS/NPPES example, why a flat 'one big table' fails Maria's compliance reporting (duplicate providers, un-attributable measures, no reusable conformed dimension).
Produce a Delta-backed dimensional skeleton in Databricks: empty typed Delta tables for fact_charge and the four dimensions with surrogate-key and audit columns, ready for population in later weeks.
lessons: Lesson 8.1 — Why dimensional modeling exists (1.5h): the analytics failure mode of the 'one big table.' Recognition-before-evaluation framing: a hiring manager reads a README that says 'monthly cost report was wrong because the same hospital appeared 3 ways' and instantly recognizes the problem. Facts = the measurable business events (a charge, a price); dimensions = the who/what/where/how context you filter and group by. Contrast with W13's 3NF source shape: sources normalize to avoid update anomalies; analytics denormalizes into conformed dimensions to make questions cheap and answers auditable. Deliberately DEFER grain and the bus matrix to W15 — this week only establishes the fact/dimension split.

Lesson 8.2 — Anatomy of a fact table (2h): additive vs. semi-additive vs. non-additive measures (a charge amount is additive; a list price is non-additive/you cannot sum it across procedures). Foreign keys to dimensions, degenerate dimensions (a claim/line id that lives on the fact with no dimension table), and why a fact row should represent one business event. Worked on CMS MRF: the 'standard_charge|gross', 'standard_charge|negotiated_dollar', and 'standard_charge|min/max' columns are candidate measures; code|1|type, payer_name and plan_name point at dimensions.

Lesson 8.3 — Anatomy of a dimension: surrogate vs. natural keys (2h): why analytics uses an integer/hash surrogate key instead of the NPI or hospital EIN directly (stability across source drift, room for SCD2 history later, protection when a natural key is dirty or duplicated). Candidate business keys in the worked data: NPI (provider), CMS Certification Number / EIN (facility), CPT/HCPCS/DRG code (procedure), payer_name+plan_name (payer). Flag that provider identity is dirty (name/address variants, duplicates) — this foreshadows the MDM closer but is NOT solved this week.

Lesson 8.4 — The Project Charter as a data product spec (1.5h): translating Maria's pain into a written problem statement, a persona sketch, and 4+ KPIs with explicit formulas and measurement grain. Documentation-as-interview-prep: each KPI is a sentence you can defend in a screen. Introduce the four project KPIs (pricing-completeness pass rate, duplicate providers collapsed, records quarantined with reason, data-freshness SLA) as the charter's north star, and map each KPI to the fact/dimensions it will need.
businessFraming: Maria, a hospital revenue-cycle analyst, publishes a monthly cost-and-compliance report that leadership and CMS auditors rely on; it is wrong because prices arrive missing and inconsistent AND the same provider shows up as several records, so charges cannot be summed or attributed. A dimensional model with conformed provider/procedure/facility/payer dimensions is the structure that makes her numbers addable, auditable, and defensible under price-transparency rules.
labSummary: Inspect the REAL messy fields in a CMS Hospital Price Transparency machine-readable file and a small NPPES pull, classify every column as fact/dimension/degenerate, design the pricing star schema (fact_charge + dim_provider/procedure/facility/payer), materialize an empty typed Delta skeleton in Databricks Free Edition, and write Project Charter v0.1 with Maria's problem statement and 4+ KPIs. This is a modeling-and-framing week: you land and profile raw data to inform the model, but you do NOT yet load the fact (that comes as silver is built in later weeks).
labSteps: 1. Land real samples. In Databricks Free Edition, run the starter scaffold to download one hospital's CMS machine-readable pricing file (pick a hospital from the CMS index) into a Bronze landing path and pull ~50 provider records from the NPPES API for that hospital's city/state. Confirm both landed with a source column and an ingest timestamp (bronze contract: raw, no transforms).

2. Profile the mess. Use the scaffold's profiling TODO to print column names, inferred types, null rates, and 5 sample values per column for BOTH sources. Write down the specific messes you observe: pipe-delimited nested charge columns, blank/negative/text-in-numeric prices, payer/plan names as free text, NPI duplicates and name/address variants across NPPES rows, and schema drift between hospital files.

3. Classify columns. Build a table (in a notebook markdown cell or CSV) with one row per source column and a verdict: FACT MEASURE, DIMENSION ATTRIBUTE, or DEGENERATE, plus a one-sentence justification. Explicitly mark additive vs. non-additive for every candidate measure (e.g., gross charge = additive per line event; list/negotiated rate = non-additive reference price).

4. Draw the star. Produce a star-schema diagram (draw.io, Excalidraw, or a Markdown table) with fact_charge at center and dim_provider, dim_procedure, dim_facility, dim_payer around it. For each dimension name the surrogate key (e.g., provider_sk) and the candidate business/natural key (NPI, CPT/HCPCS/DRG, CCN/EIN, payer_name+plan_name). Note where provider identity is dirty and flag it as a future MDM concern (do not solve it now).

5. Materialize the Delta skeleton. Complete the scaffold TODOs to CREATE empty, explicitly-typed Delta tables for fact_charge and the four dimensions in your project schema, each dimension carrying its surrogate key, business key, and audit columns (source, ingest_ts). Fact_charge carries the four dimension surrogate keys, the measure columns, and a degenerate line/charge id. Run the create cell twice to confirm it is safe to re-run (idempotent DDL: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS or CREATE OR REPLACE with empty data).

6. Write Project Charter v0.1. Using the charter template, write Maria's problem statement (<=5 sentences), a one-paragraph persona, and the 4+ KPIs each with a formula and a measurement grain. Map each KPI to the fact/dimension columns it will need so the model and the charter agree.

7. Write the 'why' note. In a decisions.md, record: why you chose surrogate keys over NPI, which columns you rejected as measures and why, one schema-drift risk you already see between hospital files, and one open question you are deferring to W15 (grain) or the MDM closer (duplicate providers). These become interview answers.

8. Self-check against acceptance. Verify column classification is complete, the diagram has all five tables with keys, all five Delta tables exist and are empty/typed, the create cell re-ran cleanly, and the charter has 4+ KPIs with formulas. Commit charter v0.1, decisions.md, the classification table, and the diagram to the project repo/folder.

title: Grain, conformed dimensions & the bus matrix
gaps: G2 — declaring and enforcing fact grain (learners default to 'primary key of the source file' and silently double-count)
G1 — designing dimensions once and reusing them across processes (conformed dimensions + the enterprise bus matrix) instead of rebuilding a new provider dim per report
objectives: Write a one-sentence grain declaration for the pricing fact (e.g. 'one row per hospital CCN x billing code x payer/plan x charge-type') and encode it as an explicit GRAIN_KEYS list in code
Prove the fact is at the declared grain by running a grain-uniqueness test that returns exactly 0 duplicate grain keys after quarantine
Build an enterprise bus matrix (business processes down the rows: pricing, claims; conformed dimensions across the columns) marking every shared dimension with an X
Design and materialize at least 2 conformed dimensions (dim_provider, dim_service) with surrogate keys and identical attributes usable by BOTH the pricing and claims processes
Update the project charter with the locked grain decision plus a 'rejected alternatives' note explaining why a coarser and a finer grain were both rejected
lessons: Declaring the grain (Kimball step 2 of 4): grain = the business event you measure, chosen BEFORE picking facts or dimensions; atomic vs summary grain; why 'the primary key of the source file' is not a grain declaration (1.5h)
The double-counting trap: additive / semi-additive / non-additive facts, and how the wrong grain makes Maria's total spend over-count when negotiated prices are stored at mixed grains (1.0h)

Conformed dimensions & the enterprise bus matrix: what 'conformed' really means (same key, same attributes, same values), drill-across queries, and why one dim_provider must serve both pricing and claims (1.5h)

Surrogate keys & degenerate dimensions for a fact at grain: natural key -> surrogate key mapping, degenerate keys that live on the fact, keeping this Type-1/static for now (SCD2 history is next week, W16) (1.0h)
businessFraming: Maria's monthly cost report double-counts because negotiated prices arrive at mixed grains (some files are one row per hospital, some per service code, some per payer), and she can't tie pricing to claims because each process built its own 'provider' table. Locking one fact grain and building conformed dimensions is what lets a single spend number survive both the CFO's cost review and a CMS compliance audit.
labSummary: Take the W14 silver pricing lines and provider rows, declare and enforce the fact grain, quarantine any row that violates it, then carve out two conformed dimensions (provider, service) that both the pricing process and a future claims process will share — proven by a bus matrix and a repeatable, idempotent rebuild.
labSteps: Write the grain declaration as ONE sentence at the top of your notebook README, then encode the same decision as a GRAIN_KEYS list in code so the sentence and the code can never drift apart

Load silver_pricing_lines from W14 and compose a single grain_key by hashing the GRAIN_KEYS columns with sha2(concat_ws('||', ...), 256), coalescing nulls to a sentinel so a missing payer doesn't silently collide
Run the grain-uniqueness test: group by grain_key, count, filter count>1; capture the violators — this MUST end at 0 for the fact to be trustworthy

Build for failure: append every grain violator to a rejected_pricing Delta table with reason='GRAIN_VIOLATION', rejected_at=current_timestamp(), and the source_file, then print a LOUD alert (row count + sample) so a bad republish is never silent

Build dim_provider conformed on NPI/CCN: select the shared attributes (npi, provider_name, org_name, city, state, taxonomy), assign a surrogate key, and write it as a Delta table — Type-1/overwrite only, no SCD2 yet

Build dim_service conformed on billing_code + code_system (CPT/HCPCS/DRG) the same way, resolving the mess where one code carries several conflicting descriptions by keeping the most frequent description per code

Rewrite the pricing fact to carry the surrogate keys (provider_sk, service_sk) plus its degenerate keys, so a drill-across from pricing to a future claims fact will join on the SAME conformed dimension keys

Author the bus matrix as a small markdown/Delta table: rows = pricing, claims (planned); columns = dim_provider, dim_service, dim_date, dim_payer; mark shared dims with X and write one sentence on what conformance buys you

Prove idempotency: run the whole notebook 10x with mode('overwrite') for the dims/fact and append-only for rejects; assert dim and fact row counts are identical across runs, then paste the counts into the charter

title: Recoverable History: SCD Type 2 & Effective Dating on the Provider and Price Dimensions
gaps: G3 (recoverable history / temporal correctness): the learner can preserve every version of a changing attribute with effective dating so any past state is reconstructable, instead of overwriting and destroying history — this week's core close.

G2 (auditability of change): the learner can answer 'what did this record look like on date X, and when did it change?' with a point-in-time query backed by an append-only audit log — seeded here, deepened when the audit log is formalized in later weeks.

Detect and handle blocking failures loudly: quarantine records with no usable blocking attribute (reason + timestamp) and flag oversized/skewed blocks that would explode the pair count.
Prove idempotency: rerun the reference + crosswalk + blocking build 10 times and assert identical dim row counts AND identical candidate-pair counts.
lessons: Reference vs. master vs. transactional data (~0.75h): the three data classes and why they live in different layers — a provider registry is reference/master data that belongs in a silver dimension, while pricing rows are transactional; the layer contract (silver = clean+conformed+historized, gold = serve-only) and where a crosswalk sits.

Crosswalks & the shared-key problem (~0.5h): what a crosswalk table is, natural vs. surrogate keys, why CMS price-transparency files almost never carry a clean NPI, and the match_status lifecycle (unmatched → candidate → resolved) that W19 will consume.

Standardization & normalization for matching (~0.75h): why raw strings never join — casefolding, punctuation/whitespace stripping, USPS street-suffix abbreviations, and phonetic encodings (soundex/metaphone); splitting NPPES entity type 1 (individual) vs 2 (organization) because they match on different attributes.

Blocking & match keys — beating N-squared (~0.75h): the combinatorial cost of all-pairs comparison, blocking predicates as a recall-vs-cost tradeoff, why you run MULTIPLE blocking passes (union of blocks) to protect recall, and how a single bad block key (e.g. state alone) creates skewed mega-blocks.

Candidate-pair generation without a cartesian (~0.5h): self-join strictly within a block, deduping symmetric pairs with an a<b ordering rule, and block-size guardrails that cap or quarantine oversized blocks before they detonate the pair count.
businessFraming: Maria's monthly cost analysis is wrong because the SAME hospital shows up as several provider records with slightly different names and addresses, so her spend and compliance rollups double-count and mislabel facilities. Before anyone can trust a single price per provider, the pipeline needs governed reference data and a defensible way to find which records are candidates for being the same entity — cheaply, at scale, and without comparing every row to every other row.

MERGE-UPSERT ON NPI (idempotent): write dim_provider_ref with Delta MERGE keyed on NPI so a rerun updates in place instead of appending. This is the deliberate idempotency choice for a reference dimension — record WHY (stable natural key) in your why-note.

# Week 18 - MDM I: reference data, crosswalks & match keys (STARTER SCAFFOLD)
# BUSINESS FRAMING: duplicate provider records make Maria's cost + compliance
# rollups double-count. This week we build governed reference data and the
# candidate pairs W19 will score. We do NOT score or merge here.

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

SILVER_NPPES   = "silver.nppes_provider"        # landed+typed from earlier weeks
SILVER_PRICING = "silver.pricing_facility"      # pricing facility rows
DIM_REF        = "silver.dim_provider_ref"
XWALK          = "silver.xwalk_provider"
PAIRS          = "silver.candidate_pairs"
REJECTED       = "silver.rejected_records"
AUDIT          = "silver.audit_log"

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1) STANDARDIZE match attributes into the reference dimension
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
src = spark.table(SILVER_NPPES)

# TODO: casefold + trim + strip punctuation on name/address columns.
#       Hint: F.upper(F.trim(F.regexp_replace(col, r"[^A-Za-z0-9 ]", "")))
# TODO: normalize USPS street suffixes (ST->STREET, AVE->AVENUE, ...).
#       Build a small mapping and apply it; do NOT hardcode one example.
# TODO: derive zip5 (validate/zero-pad) and keep state.
# TODO: split entity_type_code: 1 = individual (last/first), 2 = organization
#       (org name) -> a single std_name column chosen by entity type.
ref = (src
    .withColumn("npi", F.trim(F.col("npi")))
    # .withColumn("std_name", ...)   # TODO
    # .withColumn("std_addr", ...)   # TODO
    # .withColumn("zip5",     ...)   # TODO
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2) IDEMPOTENT upsert of the reference dimension (MERGE on NPI)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# TODO: write `ref` to DIM_REF the first run (Delta, partitionBy state),
#       then convert to a MERGE keyed on NPI so reruns update in place.
#       WHY note: NPI is a stable natural key -> MERGE, not append.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3) CROSSWALK skeleton (W19 fills match_status)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# TODO: build xwalk_provider = one row per pricing facility source record:
#       (source_system, source_record_id, npi_or_null, facility_key,
#        match_status='unmatched'). Most pricing rows have NO clean NPI.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4) BLOCKING KEYS (>=2 deterministic passes)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# TODO: block_key_1 = soundex(std_name) concat state
# TODO: block_key_2 = zip5 concat substring(std_name,1,3)
# blocked = ref.withColumn("block_key_1", ...).withColumn("block_key_2", ...)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5) QUARANTINE un-blockable records (loud, not silent)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# TODO: rows with no name AND no zip -> REJECTED with
#       reason='no_usable_block_key', ingest_ts, source. Count + audit.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 6) CANDIDATE PAIRS within blocks (NO cartesian) + skew guard
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
def pairs_for(df, key):
    # TODO: compute block sizes; flag/cap blocks over a threshold
    #       (e.g. >500) as 'oversized_block' before joining.
    a = df.select(F.col("npi").alias("id_a"), F.col(key).alias("bk"))
    b = df.select(F.col("npi").alias("id_b"), F.col(key).alias("bk"))
    return (a.join(b, "bk")
              .where(F.col("id_a") < F.col("id_b"))   # kill symmetric dups
              .withColumn("block_key", F.lit(key)))
# TODO: union pairs_for(blocked,"block_key_1") and block_key_2, dedup, write PAIRS.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 7) AUDIT + reduction ratio, then rerun 10x to prove idempotency
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# TODO: log records_standardized, records_quarantined, n_blocks,
#       oversized_blocks, candidate_pairs, reduction_ratio to AUDIT.
# TODO: run this notebook 10x; assert DIM_REF count and PAIRS count are
#       identical every run. Paste the proof into your why-note.

title: MDM II — Entity Resolution & Golden Records: collapsing duplicate providers into one trustworthy record
gaps: G2 — entity resolution: turn many messy source rows about the same real-world thing into ONE record with a stable key, using blocking + fuzzy matching + clustering rather than exact joins
G1 — data quality as a gate, not a vibe: encode survivorship/trust rules and a confidence threshold so the pipeline decides what is 'good enough to publish' vs. what a human must review
G9 — governance & stewardship: build a human-in-the-loop review queue and an auditable golden-record lineage so ownership and decisions are provable, not implicit
objectives: Given a blocked candidate set from W18, generate candidate PAIRS and score each pair with at least three similarity features (edit distance on name, address similarity, phonetic/soundex agreement) — no all-pairs cross joins
Combine feature scores into a single match confidence in [0,1] and defend a chosen AUTO-MERGE threshold and a REVIEW band with a labeled sample (precision/recall trade-off stated in words)

Cluster matched pairs into entity groups and apply written SURVIVORSHIP rules (most-recent, most-complete, source-priority) to emit exactly ONE golden record per real provider, with a stable golden_provider_id
Route every low-confidence pair to a governed human-review QUEUE table (pair, features, score, reason, timestamp, status) instead of silently guessing
Make the whole resolution idempotent: rerun 10× and prove golden-record counts, golden IDs, and the review queue are stable (MERGE on deterministic keys, no duplicate golden rows)
lessons: Entity resolution end to end (0.75h): the pipeline blocking → pairwise scoring → clustering → survivorship → golden record; why exact joins fail on real data and why NPI alone is NOT enough (same provider, multiple NPIs; one NPI reused/typo'd across files)

Fuzzy matching mechanics (0.75h): Levenshtein/edit distance vs. token-based similarity vs. phonetic (soundex) — what each catches and misses; the classic 'William→Illiam', 'St'→'Saint', 'Dr.'→'Drive', suite-number, and abbreviation problems; using Spark's built-in levenshtein() and soundex() so it runs on Free Edition with no extra installs

From feature scores to a decision (0.75h): weighting features into one confidence, choosing an auto-merge threshold and a review band, and the precision/recall trade-off framed as money/risk — a false merge hides a real facility's prices; a false split double-counts a provider in Maria's cost report

Survivorship & golden records (0.5h): clustering matched pairs into groups (connected components / transitive closure intuition), then survivorship rules (recency, completeness, source priority) and lineage — every golden field traceable to the source row it came from

Human-in-the-loop stewardship (0.5h): the review queue as a governance artifact — schema, statuses (pending/approved/rejected), why a steward's decision must be captured and fed back, and how this closes the ownership gap for a data product

Idempotency for MDM (0.25h): why golden IDs must be deterministic (hash of stable cluster members, not a monotonic surrogate that changes every run) so reruns and CMS republishes don't churn golden_provider_id
businessFraming: Maria's monthly cost analysis and CMS compliance report are wrong because the same hospital and physician group show up as several different provider records — so a facility's prices look 'missing' when they exist under a duplicate, and spend is double-counted. Collapsing duplicates into one trusted golden record per provider is what makes her numbers defensible to auditors and to Finance.
labSummary: Take the blocked candidate set your W18 SILVER job produced and turn it into GOLDEN records. Generate candidate pairs inside each block, score each pair with edit-distance, address, and phonetic features, combine them into a confidence, auto-merge high-confidence pairs into clusters, apply written survivorship rules to emit one golden record per provider, and route everything in the ambiguous middle band to a human-review queue. Prove the whole thing reruns identically 10×.
labSteps: 1. RECOGNITION README first: write the 1–2 sentence business framing (duplicate providers break Maria's cost + compliance numbers) and name the SPECIFIC mess in your candidate set — e.g. 'HCA HOUSTON HEALTHCARE' vs 'Hca Houston Health Care', 'ST LUKES' vs 'Saint Lukes', suite-number-only address differences, and one provider holding two NPIs. Paste 5 real duplicate examples pulled from NPPES.

2. Load the W18 blocked candidates from SILVER (provider records already standardized + assigned a blocking key). Within each block, generate candidate PAIRS with a self-join filtered to id_left < id_right (never a full cross join) so you compare only plausible duplicates. Log the pair count and the largest block size (watch for a runaway block).

3. Build similarity FEATURES per pair with Spark built-ins only: normalized levenshtein() on standardized name, a token/levenshtein similarity on standardized address line, and a soundex() equality flag on the last name / core name token. Add same-state and same-postal-prefix boolean features. Keep each feature in [0,1].

4. Combine features into a single match_confidence (start with a documented weighted sum — TODO in the scaffold). Hand-label ~30 pairs as true/false duplicates, then pick an AUTO-MERGE threshold and a REVIEW band (e.g. >=0.90 auto, 0.65–0.90 review, <0.65 non-match). Write ONE paragraph defending the cut in precision/recall + money terms.

5. Cluster the auto-merge pairs into entity groups (transitive closure: if A~B and B~C then A,B,C are one provider). Use an iterative min-member-id label propagation over the accepted pairs (scaffolded) and assign each cluster a DETERMINISTIC golden_provider_id = hash of the sorted stable source keys — not a monotonically increasing id.

6. Apply SURVIVORSHIP rules to pick each golden field: most-recent ingest for volatile fields (address, phone), most-complete (non-null, longest) for name, and source-priority for NPI. Emit ONE golden row per cluster to a GOLDEN Delta table, plus a golden_lineage table mapping golden_provider_id → every contributing source row + which field it won.

7. QUARANTINE + REVIEW QUEUE: write every review-band pair to a review_queue Delta table with pair ids, all feature values, match_confidence, reason ('confidence in review band'), ingest timestamp, and status='pending'. Write clearly-broken inputs (null name, malformed NPI) to the existing rejected table with reason. Emit a one-line alert with counts.

8. IDEMPOTENCY proof: MERGE golden + review rows on their deterministic keys, then run the whole notebook 10× and assert golden_provider_id set, golden row count, and review_queue count are identical every run. Capture the KPI row: # duplicates collapsed, # golden records, # pairs sent to review, % change vs last run.

9. Write the 'why' note (interview answers): why levenshtein+soundex over exact join, why THIS threshold, which survivorship rule you chose per field and the failure it prevents, and why golden IDs are hashed. Update the KPI section of the Project Charter with 'duplicate providers collapsed into golden records' for this run.

# silver_to_golden_entity_resolution.py
# Databricks Free Edition + Delta + PySpark. Run as a notebook.
# W18 produced SILVER provider records with a standardized name/address + a blocking_key.
# This week: pairs -> similarity features -> confidence -> cluster -> golden + review queue.

from pyspark.sql import functions as F, Window

SILVER = "workspace.default.silver_providers"        # standardized + blocking_key from W18
GOLDEN = "workspace.default.golden_providers"
LINEAGE = "workspace.default.golden_lineage"
REVIEW = "workspace.default.provider_review_queue"

silver = spark.table(SILVER)  # cols: src_key, npi, name_std, addr_std, state, postal, ingest_ts, source

# --- 1) Candidate PAIRS within each block (NO full cross join) ---
l = silver.alias("l"); r = silver.alias("r")
pairs = (l.join(r, (F.col("l.blocking_key") == F.col("r.blocking_key")) &
                  (F.col("l.src_key") < F.col("r.src_key")))   # dedupe + no self-pair
         .select(F.col("l.src_key").alias("key_left"), F.col("r.src_key").alias("key_right"),
                 F.col("l.name_std").alias("name_l"), F.col("r.name_std").alias("name_r"),
                 F.col("l.addr_std").alias("addr_l"), F.col("r.addr_std").alias("addr_r"),
                 F.col("l.state").alias("state_l"), F.col("r.state").alias("state_r"),
                 F.col("l.postal").alias("postal_l"), F.col("r.postal").alias("postal_r")))
# TODO: log pairs.count() and the max block size; if one block explodes, tighten the W18 blocking_key.

# --- 2) Similarity FEATURES (Spark built-ins only) ---
def norm_lev(a, b):
    # 1 - (edit_distance / max_len)  -> in [0,1]; higher = more similar
    maxlen = F.greatest(F.length(a), F.length(b), F.lit(1))
    return F.lit(1.0) - (F.levenshtein(a, b) / maxlen)

feat = (pairs
        .withColumn("f_name", norm_lev(F.col("name_l"), F.col("name_r")))
        .withColumn("f_addr", norm_lev(F.col("addr_l"), F.col("addr_r")))
        .withColumn("f_soundex", (F.soundex(F.col("name_l")) == F.soundex(F.col("name_r"))).cast("double"))
        .withColumn("f_state", (F.col("state_l") == F.col("state_r")).cast("double")))
# TODO: add a postal-prefix feature and, if you like, a token-overlap feature for org names.

# --- 3) Combine into ONE confidence (defend your weights) ---
# TODO: replace this naive equal weighting after you hand-label ~30 pairs.
conf = feat.withColumn("match_confidence",
        (F.col("f_name")*0.4 + F.col("f_addr")*0.3 + F.col("f_soundex")*0.2 + F.col("f_state")*0.1))

# --- 4) DECISION bands ---
AUTO, REVIEW_LO = 0.90, 0.65   # TODO: justify these from your labeled sample (precision vs recall).
accepted = conf.filter(F.col("match_confidence") >= AUTO)
to_review = conf.filter((F.col("match_confidence") >= REVIEW_LO) & (F.col("match_confidence") < AUTO))

# --- 5) CLUSTER accepted pairs into entity groups (transitive closure) ---
# TODO: implement iterative label propagation: each node's label = min(own, neighbors');
#       iterate until labels stop changing. Then golden_provider_id = a DETERMINISTIC hash of
#       the sorted src_keys in the cluster (F.sha2), NOT monotonically_increasing_id().

# --- 6) SURVIVORSHIP -> one golden row per cluster ---
# TODO: per golden_provider_id, choose fields by rule:
#       address/phone = most-recent ingest_ts; name = most-complete (longest non-null);
#       npi = source-priority. Write GOLDEN, and write LINEAGE (golden_id -> src_key -> field_won).

# --- 7) REVIEW QUEUE (governance artifact) ---
review_rows = (to_review
    .withColumn("reason", F.lit("confidence_in_review_band"))
    .withColumn("status", F.lit("pending"))
    .withColumn("queued_ts", F.current_timestamp()))
# TODO: MERGE review_rows into REVIEW on (key_left, key_right) so reruns don't duplicate the queue.

# --- 8) IDEMPOTENCY ---
# TODO: MERGE golden + lineage on their deterministic keys; then run this notebook 10x and assert
#       golden count, golden_provider_id set, and REVIEW count are identical every run.

# --- KPI line for the Charter ---

This week converts the medallion metaphor into WRITTEN, TESTED layer contracts (bronze=raw landed only; silver=clean+conform+historize; gold=serve-only) with automated assertions that FAIL LOUD when a layer does work that belongs to another.

G2 (seeds): conformance and typing rigor — learners tend to trust the raw strings CMS/NPPES hand them. This week seeds the discipline of never reading a business value straight from bronze: casting, trimming, code/unit standardization, and a documented primary-key grain all become a silver-contract requirement (the full historize/SCD2 build lands later; here we define the contract and the typing/conform half of it).

Implement at least 3 automated contract assertions on the W21 project bronze (required ingest-metadata columns present; payload columns still raw/StringType; row count only ever grows append-only) that raise a loud, named error on violation.

Build a thin silver-conform step that types, trims, and standardizes at least 4 fields (charge decimal, provider name, 2-letter state, zero-padded ZIP) and declares the silver primary-key grain in writing.
Route every row that fails the silver contract to a rejected table with a specific _reject_reason + _reject_ts (zero silent drops), and prove passed+rejected = input count.
Expose gold as a serve-only VIEW over silver and demonstrate (by a failing test) that adding any cleaning logic in gold violates the contract.
lessons: Medallion as CONTRACTS, not folders (45 min): why bronze/silver/gold exist, what each layer promises its consumers, and how a leaked transform (casting in bronze, re-cleaning in gold) silently destroys reproducibility and auditability. Frame each layer as a contract with a producer and a consumer.

The bronze contract — raw, append-only, provenance (40 min): source file, ingest timestamp, source system; why bronze must stay untyped/unfiltered so you can always replay history and prove what CMS actually published on a given day.

The silver contract — clean + conform + (later) historize (55 min): typing, trimming, code/unit standardization, choosing and documenting the PRIMARY-KEY GRAIN, quality gates, and quarantine. We build the clean+conform half now; SCD2/CDC historize is flagged as the W23+ extension so silver stays honest.

The gold contract — serve-only (30 min): business-ready marts/KPIs read from silver ONLY; no cleaning allowed downstream of silver; why 'if you need to clean it in gold, it belongs in silver' is the enforcement rule.

businessFraming: Maria's finance team keeps re-cleaning the same hospital pricing data in three different reports because nobody agreed on where cleaning happens — so two dashboards show different total charges for the same provider and compliance can't tell which number is defensible. title: Spark internals — partitions, shuffles, skew & the Spark UI
gaps: G7 — The learner can run Spark jobs but cannot read the Spark UI to explain WHY one is slow. They can't locate the expensive stage, spot a straggler task, or interpret shuffle read/write and task-time distribution. This week CLOSES it with hands-on, UI-driven diagnosis of a real slow job.

G9 — The learner treats Spark as a black box with no mental model of partitions, shuffles, or data skew, so 'make it faster' becomes guessing (bigger cluster, more partitions, random config flags). This week SEEDS the internals model (partition = unit of parallelism; shuffle = the expensive redistribution; skew = a few hot keys) and installs the 'measure first, tune second' habit that later performance weeks build on.
objectives: Read the Spark UI to locate a skewed stage: identify the straggler task whose duration and shuffle-read are >=10x the stage median, and name the exact join/stage causing it (not just 'the job is slow').

Explain and predict partitioning behavior: state how many shuffle partitions a join will produce from spark.sql.shuffle.partitions, and compute per-key row counts to prove which blocking keys are hot.

Apply and MEASURE two skew remedies on the provider-dedup join — salting the hot blocking key and broadcasting the small side — recording before/after wall-clock and max-task time, and achieving a >=2x reduction in the skewed stage's max-task time.

Decide when Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) skew-join handling is sufficient versus when manual salting/broadcast is required, and justify the decision in writing with evidence from an AQE-off vs AQE-on comparison.
Prove a performance fix preserved correctness: assert the candidate-pair output count is identical before and after tuning (a faster wrong answer is not a fix).
lessons: Partitions 101 — how Spark splits data into partitions as the unit of parallelism; input partitions vs shuffle partitions; the role of spark.sql.shuffle.partitions; why partition count sets the ceiling on parallelism and why 'too few' and 'too many' both hurt. (1.0h)

The shuffle — what operations trigger it (joins, groupBy, distinct, window), why moving data across the cluster is the single most expensive thing Spark does, and how to read shuffle read/write bytes and records in the Spark UI stage detail. (1.0h)

Data skew — the difference between 'big' and 'skewed'; how a handful of hot keys (a few giant health systems) send millions of rows to ONE partition and create a straggler task while every other core sits idle; spotting it via the event timeline, the task summary (min/median/max), and the largest-task metrics. (1.0h)

Remedies and when each applies — broadcast join and spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (kill the shuffle on the small side); salting a skewed key to spread one hot key across N partitions; and AQE skew-join splitting that Databricks does automatically. Trade-offs: broadcast needs a genuinely small side; salting adds work and must replicate the other side; AQE helps joins but not every case. (1.0h)

Measure first — how to baseline a job, isolate the one stage that matters, and read a before/after honestly; why tuning blind (more cores, more partitions, copied Stack Overflow flags) wastes money and hides the real bottleneck. (0.5h)
businessFraming: Maria's monthly dedup now stalls: the provider-matching join finishes only after one giant task grinds on a handful of mega health systems, and the run risks blowing past the data-freshness SLA — meaning her compliance report ships on stale prices or misses its filing window, and an oversized always-on cluster burns budget to hide the problem. A pipeline that is slow-but-silent on a straggler is exactly how a monthly close quietly starts missing deadlines.
labSummary: Take the provider-dedup candidate-pair join you built in W26 and make it FAST without making it WRONG. You will baseline it, use the Spark UI to prove the slowness is data skew from a few dominant health systems, apply salting and broadcast fixes, compare against Databricks' automatic AQE skew handling, and write a one-page before/after diagnosis that goes straight into your architecture doc. The whole lab is an exercise in 'measure first': every claim is backed by a Spark UI screenshot and a timing number, and every fix is proven to leave the join output unchanged.
labSteps: Reproduce your W26 candidate-pair dedup self-join on your silver provider table and run it once end-to-end to establish a BASELINE; force execution (e.g. .count()) and record wall-clock time and the shuffle-partition setting you used.

Profile the blocking key: groupBy(block_key).count().orderBy(desc) and show the top 20. Name the SPECIFIC health systems (e.g. HCA, Kaiser, Ascension, Ascension-affiliated NPIs) whose thousands of provider records create the hot keys — write the counts down.

Turn AQE OFF (spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=false) so the raw skew is visible, open the Spark UI, find the join stage, and identify the straggler: capture max vs median task time, the largest task's shuffle-read bytes, and a screenshot of the event timeline showing one long task while others finish early.

Apply Fix A — salting: add a random salt 0..N-1 to the left side of the hot key and replicate the right side across all N salt values; pick N DELIBERATELY (try a couple of values), re-run, and record the new max-task time and wall-clock.

Apply Fix B — broadcast: identify a genuinely small side (the CMS price-transparency hospital list, or a filtered provider subset under the broadcast threshold), wrap it in F.broadcast(), re-run the join, and record timing — noting that this eliminates the shuffle entirely rather than reshaping it.

Turn AQE back ON and re-run the untouched baseline to see whether Databricks' automatic skew-join splitting alone closes the gap; assemble all four runs (baseline AQE-off, salt, broadcast, baseline AQE-on) into a single before/after runtime table.

Correctness gate: assert the candidate-pair row count is IDENTICAL across the baseline and every fixed version; if a fix changes the count, it changed the join semantics and is rejected regardless of speed.

Write the one-page 'Skew Diagnosis & Fix' note (before/after screenshots, the runtime table, the named hot keys, the chosen remedy and why over the alternatives, and the AQE on/off verdict) and append it as the performance section of your 4-part architecture doc.

datasets.name: NPPES bulk data files (monthly full NPI dump)
datasets.whatsMessy: Millions of rows (~9GB uncompressed) — big enough to produce REAL skew on Free Edition. Large health systems (HCA, Kaiser, Ascension, CommonSpirit) own thousands of individual NPIs that share the same organization-name token + state, so any blocking key built on org-name+state sends millions of candidate pairs to a single partition. Mixed casing, abbreviations ('DEPT' vs 'DEPARTMENT'), PO-box vs street addresses, and reused org names across affiliates all inflate the hot keys.

title: Data quality I — expectations & quarantine: making silver break loudly
gaps: G4 — Learner treats data quality as an afterthought (a final SELECT COUNT of NULLs) rather than an enforced, testable contract; cannot articulate WHICH specific rules protect a business KPI, cannot route bad rows anywhere but /dev/null, and has no threshold-based alerting — so pipelines fail silently and downstream trust erodes.
objectives: Given the project silver provider+pricing table, WRITE at least 8 specific, named expectations across four rule classes (schema/type, not-null, uniqueness, domain/accepted-code) and justify each in one sentence tied to a KPI or compliance need — no boilerplate 'column should not be null'.

IMPLEMENT a validation pass in PySpark/Spark SQL that TAGS each row pass/fail per rule and SPLITS the DataFrame into a clean stream and a quarantine stream without dropping any input row (row-count in == clean + rejected).

PERSIST rejected rows to a Delta `silver_rejected` table carrying failure_reason(s), the rule id, the offending value, source file, and a rejected_at timestamp — queryable so a human can triage why a row failed.

COMPUTE per-run DQ metrics (rows in, rows passed, rows quarantined, % pass per rule) and FIRE a threshold alert (raise/log an alert row) when the quarantine rate for any rule exceeds a declared budget (e.g. > 5%).
PROVE the DQ step is idempotent by running it 10× on the same input and showing identical clean and rejected counts (MERGE/overwrite-partition keyed on run, not blind append).
lessons: Expectations as a data contract (0.75h): the difference between a check and a contract — a named rule + severity (warn vs. fail) + owner + a business reason. Map the four rule classes (schema/type conformance, null/completeness, uniqueness/grain, domain/accepted-code) onto the project's NPI, CPT/HCPCS code, and gross/negotiated price columns.

Quarantine architecture & the flag-then-split pattern (1.0h): why you TAG rows before you split (so one row can fail multiple rules and you keep the audit), the anatomy of a `silver_rejected` table (natural key + full offending payload + reason array + rule id + rejected_at + source_file + run_id), and why quarantine beats dropping or halting — 'silent is worse than loud'.

Severity, thresholds & alerting (0.75h): warn-vs-fail severities, per-rule quarantine budgets, and computing a run-level DQ summary; turning a breached threshold into an ALERT (alert row + printed/loud failure) vs. letting the run continue. Introduces the idea of a data-freshness/completeness SLA feeding the project KPI '% facilities passing pricing-completeness'.

Idempotent DQ runs (0.5h): why re-running validation must not double-count rejects — keying rejected/summary writes on run_id and using overwrite-partition or MERGE; how this connects to W27's understanding of Spark actions and shuffle so metrics are computed once, not recomputed inconsistently.
businessFraming: Maria's monthly cost analysis and the hospital's federally-required price-transparency compliance report are only as trustworthy as the silver table feeding them — and right now a single malformed price or an out-of-range CPT code silently poisons a KPI that a compliance officer signs their name to. This week builds the gate that catches those rows loudly, quarantines them with a reason, and alerts before bad data reaches a regulator-facing number.
labSummary: You extend the project's SILVER layer with an enforced data-quality gate. Starting from your conformed silver provider+pricing table (from earlier weeks) plus a small deck of intentionally bad rows you inject, you declare 8+ named expectations, implement a flag-then-split validator in PySpark, land failures in a Delta `silver_rejected` table with reasons and timestamps, compute a per-run DQ summary, fire a threshold alert when any rule's quarantine rate exceeds its budget, and prove the whole step is idempotent across 10 reruns. The clean stream continues down the pipeline; nothing is silently dropped.
labSteps: Assemble your test input: take your existing silver provider+pricing DataFrame and UNION a small hand-crafted 'bad-row deck' (10–20 rows) that violates each rule class on purpose — a null/blank NPI, a 9-digit NPI, a duplicate (npi, cpt_code) grain collision, a negotiated_price of -1 and one that is a string like 'N/A', a cpt_code not in your accepted-code set, a mangled payer name. Tag these so you can later confirm every planted row was caught.

Write your expectations catalog as a Python list/dict of named rules — each with rule_id, target column(s), rule_class, severity (warn|fail), a Spark boolean expression, and a one-line business reason. Aim for 8+: e.g. NPI is exactly 10 digits (schema), NPI not null (completeness), (npi, cpt_code) unique (grain), cpt_code in accepted set (domain), gross_charge/negotiated_price are numeric and >= 0 (domain), payer_name not blank (completeness).

Implement the flag pass: loop the catalog and add one boolean column per rule (`dq__<rule_id>` = true when the row PASSES). Add a `dq_failed_rules` array column collecting the rule_ids that failed, and a `dq_is_valid` = size(dq_failed_rules)==0. Do NOT filter yet — every input row still present. Assert row_count unchanged.

Split the stream: clean = rows where dq_is_valid; rejected = rows where NOT dq_is_valid. For rejected, build the quarantine payload — original columns + dq_failed_rules (reason array) + first offending rule_id + rejected_at = current_timestamp() + source_file + run_id. Verify clean.count() + rejected.count() == input.count().

Persist rejected rows to Delta table `silver_rejected`, partitioned by (or keyed on) run_id, using overwrite-partition or MERGE on run_id so a rerun replaces that run's rejects rather than appending duplicates. Write the clean stream forward to your silver table for the run.

Compute the DQ run summary: rows_in, rows_passed, rows_quarantined, and per-rule pass_rate (%). Write it to a `dq_run_summary` Delta table keyed on run_id. This % pass feeds the project KPI '% facilities passing the pricing-completeness check per run'.

Implement the threshold alert: for each rule with severity=fail, if its quarantine rate exceeds its declared budget (e.g. > 5%), emit an alert — append an `dq_alerts` row (run_id, rule_id, observed_rate, budget, fired_at) AND raise/print a loud, unmissable message. Decide deliberately: does a breach halt the run or continue with alert? Write your choice in the why-note.

  watermark_value STRING, control_total_num DECIMAL(18,2), distinct_key_count LONG,

Prove idempotency with an automated test that runs the full pipeline twice on a fixture and asserts identical row counts AND identical golden-record counts (not a prose claim)

lessons: The testing pyramid for DATA pipelines (~1.0h): why data tests differ from app tests (the input mutates underneath you), the four tiers and what each buys you, and the data-specific test families layered on top — schema/contract tests, PK-uniqueness, referential integrity, quarantine-reason coverage, and freshness. Map each tier to a piece of your existing pipeline.

pytest mechanics on Databricks Free Edition (~1.0h): the anatomy of a test (arrange/act/assert), a session-scoped SparkSession fixture in conftest.py, @pytest.fixture for tiny deterministic data, @pytest.mark.parametrize for table-driven cases, tmp_path for throwaway Delta tables, chispa for DataFrame equality, and running pytest.main() inside a notebook vs. a .py module.

Testing for failure & idempotency (~0.75h): writing NEGATIVE tests (feed a bad row, assert it lands in the rejected table with reason+timestamp), asserting SCD2 close/open on an updated record, and the run-twice idempotency assertion pattern — the same discipline you eyeballed in earlier weeks, now encoded so it fails loudly in CI.

Portfolio assembly & the recognition test (~0.75h): README structure that front-loads business framing, reporting KPIs as real numbers with a small results table, the ‘prove a human did the work’ why-notes, and cross-linking the charter + 4-part architecture doc + golden records so the whole thing reads as one owned data product.
businessFraming: Maria's finance leadership will only act on the cost + compliance numbers if they trust them; a silent regression (a parser that starts dropping every "$1,234.00" price, or a dedupe that quietly stops collapsing providers) would push wrong numbers into a board deck and a CMS compliance filing. Automated tests are how you promise that next month's rerun is still correct without re-inspecting it by hand.
labSummary: Retrofit a real pytest suite onto the complete Provider Pricing Integrity pipeline, organized by the four-tier taxonomy, then assemble the finished Phase 2 portfolio. You refactor silver transforms into importable pure functions, freeze a tiny deterministic fixture that carries the CMS/NPPES mess (null price, "$"-string price, late record, duplicate provider), write unit/integration/smoke/e2e tests that encode your quarantine, SCD2, contract, and idempotency guarantees, run the full pipeline on real data to capture the four KPIs as numbers, and ship a recognition-ready README plus locked charter and architecture doc.
labSteps: Freeze fixtures: extract a ~50-row deterministic sample from your bronze CMS price + NPPES data into tests/fixtures/ (parquet or hardcoded rows) so tests never hit the network. It MUST contain at least one null price, one '$1,234.00'-formatted string price, one late-arriving record (older ingest date than its key already has), and one duplicate provider spelled/addressed two ways for the MDM test.

Refactor for testability: pull your silver logic (price parsing, NPI normalization, address standardization, quarantine-reason tagging) out of notebook cells into pure importable functions in a transforms.py module — functions that take/return values or small DataFrames with no hidden I/O.

Write ≥3 UNIT tests (@pytest.mark.parametrize): '$1,234.00' → 1234.00, ''/null price → quarantine reason 'MISSING_PRICE', and NPI '  1234567890 ' → '1234567890'. These run in milliseconds with no Spark table.

Write ≥2 INTEGRATION tests on the fixture (bronze→silver): assert bad rows land in the rejected table with reason + timestamp (and are absent from silver), and assert that re-ingesting an updated provider closes the prior SCD2 row (is_current=false, valid_to set) and opens exactly one new current row.

Write 1 SMOKE test: run the pipeline end-to-end on the fixture and assert the silver/gold schema matches your written layer contract, the golden_provider_id PK is unique and non-null, and every output layer is non-empty — the fast 'is it alive and shaped right' check.

Write ≥2 E2E tests: run ingest→bronze→silver→golden→gold on the fixture, assert the 4 KPIs are computed and sane; then run the ENTIRE pipeline a SECOND time and assert identical row counts and identical golden-record count — idempotency proven, not claimed.

Run `pytest -v`, capture the green output, then execute one real full-data pipeline run and record the four KPIs as actual numbers: % facilities passing the completeness check, # duplicate providers collapsed into golden records, # records quarantined broken out by reason, and the data-freshness SLA figure.

Assemble the portfolio: finalize README (business framing → architecture diagram → KPI results table → how-to-run → test suite summary), lock the project charter and the 4-part architecture doc, cross-link both to the test suite and golden-records table, and write the short 'why we test at each tier + why these idempotency choices' note that becomes your interview answers.

liveRecap: Open by screen-sharing your green `pytest -v` output and reading your KPI results table out loud in plain business terms: 'X% of facilities pass the pricing-completeness check, we collapsed N duplicate providers into golden records, we quarantined M records — here's the reason breakdown — and our freshness SLA is T.' Then walk one test from each tier and say what real regression it would catch.
liveMisconception: 'More assert statements in a notebook = tested.' The four tiers are not decoration — they trade off speed vs. coverage vs. confidence, and a test only counts if it can FAIL: a green suite that still passes after you break the parser is testing nothing. Likewise, 'idempotent' and 'quarantines bad rows' are properties you must encode as tests that run twice / feed a bad row, not sentences in a README.
liveHotSeat: Defend your test design: (1) Point to one test in each tier and justify why it lives at that tier and not another. (2) Which single test would you keep if you could keep only one, and why? (3) Show the assertion that proves idempotency — and explain the mechanism (MERGE on key / partition replace / overwrite) it protects and why you chose it here. (4) Name one real regression each of your integration tests would catch that a unit test could not. Expect the reviewer to break your parser live and demand that a test go red.
